title: Pay-per-page newspaper archive
problem: Local papers sit on decades of archives nobody can reach without a full subscription.
challenge: Pricing a single 1987 article so it is worth selling, and worth buying.
direction: A paid API serving archive pages per request, with an agent that buys only the pages a researcher needs.
angles: What if the buyer is a historian’s agent working overnight?
Could many tiny purchases earn more than a few subscriptions?

title: A second opinion for clinic triage
problem: Rural clinics wait days for specialist input on routine cases.
challenge: The agent must decide when a paid specialist model is worth the money, and when it is not.
direction: A Python agent that triages cases and pays per call for specialist analysis, inside a daily clinic budget.
angles: How do you show a clinician why money was spent?
What happens when the budget runs out mid-shift?

title: Overnight lab instrument market
problem: Expensive lab equipment sits idle overnight while other labs queue for weeks.
challenge: Matching availability, calibration needs and price without a human in the loop.
direction: A service where instruments publish slots and booking agents place small paid holds.
angles: Could unused slots be priced like airline seats?
What if the instrument itself were the seller?

title: Revision tutor that pays per question
problem: Students hunt across dozens of sites for the right practice questions.
challenge: Paying authors fairly per question used, not per bundle.
direction: An Android tutor that fetches individual paid questions, with a weekly allowance the student sets.
angles: What if teachers earned every time their question helped?
Could the app spend more on topics you keep getting wrong?

title: Menu reader for low-vision diners
problem: Blind and low-vision diners rely on staff to read menus aloud.
challenge: It has to be fast, private and cost pennies per visit.
direction: Photograph a menu; Gemini describes it, and a paid allergen lookup runs per dish.
angles: What would a restaurant pay to be readable by default?
Could it work for medicine labels too?

title: Freight quotes without the email chains
problem: Small exporters spend hours emailing carriers for quotes.
challenge: Comparing paid quote services without overspending on the lookups themselves.
direction: An agent that queries several carriers’ paid quote endpoints within a strict lookup budget.
angles: When should the agent stop searching and book?
What if carriers bid against each other in real time?

title: Micro-licences for game mods
problem: Mod creators rarely get paid; players will not subscribe for one asset.
challenge: Making a 20p payment feel like a single tap.
direction: A web marketplace with per-download payments and a creator dashboard.
angles: Could a mod earn every time someone streams with it?
What if players could tip mid-game?

title: A tip jar for open datasets
problem: Open datasets cost money to host but rarely receive support.
challenge: Asking for payment without ever blocking open access.
direction: An API that is free under a rate limit and politely asks for payment above it.
angles: Could heavy users fund light users automatically?
What if citations triggered a thank-you payment?

title: Train disruption concierge
problem: When a train is cancelled, travellers juggle five apps to rebook.
challenge: Acting fast while respecting a hard spending cap the traveller set in advance.
direction: An agent that watches disruption feeds, pays for live availability and proposes options.
angles: Should the agent book without asking if it is cheaper?
What would a student version with a £20 cap look like?

title: Pay-as-you-listen lectures
problem: Public lecture recordings are often locked behind full course enrolment.
challenge: Charging per chapter without making listeners feel watched by a meter.
direction: A web player that unlocks chapters with tiny payments and refunds unwatched time.
angles: What if the lecturer set the price live?
Could alumni sponsor chapters for current students?

title: Price tags agents can read
problem: Shopping agents scrape pages built for humans, and badly.
challenge: Designing a product feed agents will happily pay to query.
direction: An API for independent shops that sells structured, live stock and price data per query.
angles: Should agents pay more for fresher data?
What if shops paid agents to be considered?

title: Fact-check fund for breaking news
problem: Newsrooms cannot afford to verify every claim in a fast-moving story.
challenge: The agent must choose which claims justify paid verification.
direction: An agent that scores claims, buys verification for the riskiest, and logs every spend.
angles: How do readers see what was checked?
Could readers fund checks on stories they care about?

title: Split the studio before you leave
problem: Bands splitting rehearsal-room costs chase each other for money afterwards.
challenge: Settling instantly and fairly, even when someone leaves early.
direction: An Android app that splits the booking at the moment it is paid.
angles: What if the room charged by the minute?
Could it handle a band that never pays on time?

title: Translation on demand for clinics
problem: Clinics need short translations of discharge notes at odd hours.
challenge: Paying per request while guaranteeing quality and privacy.
direction: A paid API that routes requests to the right translator (human or AI) with a quality guarantee.
angles: What if urgency set the price?
Could patients choose a human translator for a small extra fee?

title: GPU time for student researchers
problem: Students run out of compute credits halfway through experiments.
challenge: Supervisors set limits; students pay per job without paperwork.
direction: A dashboard that funds training jobs from a shared budget with spending controls.
angles: Should failed jobs be refunded automatically?
Could labs lend spare credits to each other?

title: Courier hand-off marketplace
problem: Last-mile parcels pass between couriers with no instant settlement.
challenge: Matching, proof of hand-off and payment in one step.
direction: A service that matches couriers to legs and releases payment when the hand-off is confirmed.
angles: What if the parcel paid its own way?
Could bikes and vans compete for the same leg?

title: Sign-language clip library
problem: Developers lack affordable, properly licensed sign-language video.
challenge: Licensing per clip while paying the signers fairly.
direction: An API selling clips per request, with signers paid on every use.
angles: Could regional dialects be first-class?
What if apps paid only when a clip was actually watched?

title: Teen allowance agent
problem: Teenagers have no safe way to learn how autonomous spending works.
challenge: Parent-set rules the agent can never break.
direction: An Android app with spending controls visible to both parent and teen.
angles: What if the teen could propose rule changes?
Could it teach budgeting by showing what the agent declined?

title: Weather-triggered event cover
problem: Event organisers forget weather cover until it is too late.
challenge: Deciding when forecast data is worth buying, and when to quote.
direction: An agent that buys forecasts as the date nears and prepares a quote at the right moment.
angles: Should the price change hour by hour?
Could a village fête and a festival use the same model?

title: Speedrun bounty board
problem: Communities pool small prizes for challenges but settle them by hand.
challenge: Verifying the winner fairly and paying out instantly.
direction: A web board where anyone can add to a bounty and the winner is paid on verification.
angles: What if viewers could raise the bounty live?
How would you handle a tie?

title: Citation hunter
problem: Students lose hours tracing the original source behind a statistic.
challenge: Paying for access to specific papers only when they are truly needed.
direction: An agent that follows a claim back to its source and buys single-paper access within a budget.
angles: Should it stop at the first credible source?
What if it built a shared library for a whole class?

title: Live bus data that pays for itself
problem: Bus data in smaller towns is unreliable because nobody funds it.
challenge: Letting operators earn from accurate, live data.
direction: An API selling live vehicle positions per query, with revenue shared back to operators.
angles: Should late buses earn less?
Could passengers contribute data and get paid?

title: Thirty-second human judgement
problem: AI agents sometimes need a human for a tiny decision.
challenge: Matching, quality control and instant payment for very small tasks.
direction: A service where agents post paid micro-tasks and people earn per answer.
angles: How do you price a decision that takes 30 seconds?
What if the agent paid more for faster answers?

title: Unlock one page of the repair manual
problem: Fixing a device often needs one page of a manual sold as a £30 bundle.
challenge: Selling a single procedure, with diagrams, straight to a phone.
direction: An Android app that buys only the repair steps you need, when you need them.
angles: What if repair cafés got a cut?
Could the app refund you if the fix did not work?

title: Medicine shortage scout
problem: Patients ring pharmacy after pharmacy when a common prescription is out of stock locally.
challenge: Deciding how many paid stock checks are worth it before simply waiting a day.
direction: A Python agent that pays per stock query to nearby pharmacy services, stopping once it finds the medicine or hits a small cap.
angles: What if pharmacies earned more for answering quickly?
Could the agent buy a forecast of tomorrow's stock instead of today's?

title: Physio form check per rep
problem: People doing home physiotherapy exercises rarely know whether their form is right between appointments.
challenge: Giving useful feedback on a phone video without pretending to be a physiotherapist.
direction: An Android app that films a set and pays a few cents per AI form check, with a weekly limit the patient chooses.
angles: What if the physio could top up the allowance remotely?
Could you only pay when the AI spots something worth fixing?

title: Trial-matching agent for patient groups
problem: Patient charities struggle to tell members which research studies they might be eligible to join.
challenge: Querying several paid registries without ever sending more personal detail than each one needs.
direction: A Python agent that buys eligibility checks per query from registry services, on the charity's monthly budget, and reports plain-language matches.
angles: How would a member see exactly what was shared and why?
What if the studies paid for the matching instead?

title: Discharge letter decoder
problem: Patients leave hospital with letters full of abbreviations they are too tired to look up.
challenge: Explaining clearly while always pointing back to the clinical team for decisions.
direction: A Next.js web app where a hospital charity sponsors each plain-English explanation, paid per letter decoded.
angles: What if relatives could ask follow-up questions on the same letter?
Could the charity see which phrases confuse people most?

title: Shared care costs for siblings
problem: Siblings caring for an ageing parent argue over who paid for which visit, prescription or taxi.
challenge: Making splits feel fair when siblings contribute time as well as money.
direction: An Android app that splits each small care cost instantly between siblings, with an AI summary of the month.
angles: What if hours of care counted as contributions too?
Could the parent see a gentle, guilt-free version?

title: Symptom diaries that pay patients back
problem: Researchers want real-world symptom diaries, but patients rarely see any benefit from sharing them.
challenge: Paying per anonymised entry used while keeping consent revocable at any time.
direction: A paid API that releases consented, anonymised diary entries to approved studies and pays the patient a micro-fee per entry used.
angles: What happens to past payments if someone withdraws consent?
Could patients choose to donate their earnings to a charity instead?

title: Locum shift-cover bounties
problem: Small practices scramble by phone to fill last-minute gaps in their rota.
challenge: Raising the bounty fairly as the shift gets closer without encouraging gaming.
direction: A Next.js web board where practices post a cover bounty that grows over time and releases on confirmation the shift was worked.
angles: What if neighbouring practices could chip in to a shared gap?
Could an AI predict which gaps will need a bigger bounty?

title: Scrub faces from clinical photos
problem: Clinicians want to share wound or skin photos for teaching but must remove identifying features first.
challenge: Proving an image is properly de-identified before anyone pays for it.
direction: A paid API that charges per image to blur faces, tattoos and backgrounds, refunding automatically if a reviewer flags a miss.
angles: What if teaching libraries paid the contributing clinician per view?
Could the service charge more for harder images?

title: Evidence digest for ward protocols
problem: Ward teams rarely have time to check whether new research changes their local protocols.
challenge: Choosing which papers are worth buying full text for from abstracts alone.
direction: A Python agent that pays per summary and per full-text access overnight, producing a short weekly digest within a fixed budget.
angles: How does the team challenge a summary they disagree with?
What if several wards pooled one budget and shared the digest?

title: Peer review paid by the paragraph
problem: Peer reviewers work unpaid and journals wait months for reviews to arrive.
challenge: Paying for useful comments rather than for volume of words.
direction: A Next.js web app where editors release small payments per reviewed section, weighted by whether authors found the comment useful.
angles: What if authors could tip a reviewer whose comment saved the paper?
Could an AI spot reviews that were clearly rushed?

title: Reproduce-this-result bounties
problem: Many published findings are never independently repeated because nobody funds the effort.
challenge: Agreeing in advance what counts as a successful (or failed) replication.
direction: A Next.js web app where funders pool a bounty that is held and released only when an agreed replication report is accepted.
angles: Should a careful failed replication earn the same as a success?
What if the original authors could add to the pot?

title: Amateur telescope time by the minute
problem: Remote observatories sit idle on clear nights while amateur astronomers cannot afford full sessions.
challenge: Streaming payment that stops the moment clouds roll in.
direction: An Android app that controls a shared remote telescope and pays per minute of usable sky, pausing automatically when conditions drop.
angles: What if schools got the cloudy minutes for free?
Could unused clear minutes be auctioned at the last second?

title: Budgeted molecule screening agent
problem: Small labs cannot afford to run every candidate molecule through expensive prediction models.
challenge: Spending more on promising candidates and quitting early on dead ends.
direction: A Python agent that buys structure predictions per molecule from paid model services, reallocating its budget as results arrive.
angles: How would you show a supervisor where each pound went?
What if two cheap models agreeing meant skipping the expensive one?

title: Beetle photos, paid per verified ID
problem: Biodiversity surveys need far more labelled insect photos than researchers can gather themselves.
challenge: Paying only for identifications experts or AI can confidently confirm.
direction: An Android app where walkers snap insects and earn a micro-payment from a research fund for each verified identification.
angles: What if rare species paid more, would that tempt cheating?
Could users spend their earnings on extra species guides?

title: Lab protocol steps licensed per use
problem: Researchers who refine lab techniques get little credit when others copy their protocols.
challenge: Pricing a single tweak to a method so people still use it.
direction: A paid API serving individual protocol steps per request, with each author earning a tiny fee whenever their step is fetched.
angles: What if a step's price fell as more labs confirmed it works?
Could students access everything free through a department sponsor?

title: Seismometer data priced per second
problem: Hobbyist seismometers record useful data that researchers never see.
challenge: Pricing a stream that is dull for weeks then suddenly valuable.
direction: A paid API that streams readings from volunteer stations and charges per second of data, paying station owners automatically.
angles: Should a reading during an earthquake cost more or less?
What if a researcher's agent subscribed only when activity spikes?

title: Overnight preprint triage
problem: PhD students wake to dozens of new preprints and no time to skim them.
challenge: Ranking by relevance to one student's thesis, not by popularity.
direction: A Python agent that pays per AI summary for new preprints overnight and stops at a small nightly allowance.
angles: What if the supervisor's agent shared its picks?
Could the student pay more for papers that cite their own work?

title: Thank-you tips for research software
problem: The small tools behind many papers are maintained by volunteers who never see thanks.
challenge: Making tipping as easy as adding a citation.
direction: A Next.js web app where researchers tip the tools listed in their project, split automatically among maintainers.
angles: What if a grant automatically tipped every tool a project used?
Could a tip unlock a priority bug fix?

title: Essay feedback with a refund button
problem: Students pay for essay feedback that turns out to be generic and unhelpful.
challenge: Designing a refund rule that is fair to students and feedback givers.
direction: A Next.js web app that charges per paragraph of AI feedback and refunds instantly if the student marks it unhelpful.
angles: What if refunds trained the feedback to improve?
Could tutors bid to give human feedback on the hardest paragraphs?

title: Conversation practice by the minute
problem: Language learners avoid speaking practice because lessons are booked in costly hour-long blocks.
challenge: Making per-minute payment feel relaxed rather than like a ticking clock.
direction: An Android app that streams tiny payments per minute of AI or human conversation, stopping the second the learner hangs up.
angles: What if the price fell the longer you stayed in the language?
Could two learners teach each other and settle the difference?

title: Marking agent that shops for second markers
problem: Departments struggle to find second markers for coursework at peak times.
challenge: Knowing when an AI second mark is enough and when a human must look.
direction: A Python agent that buys AI second marks per script and pays human markers only for disputed ones, within a department budget.
angles: How should a student see that their script was double-checked?
What if markers set their own per-script rate?

title: Lesson slides licensed per lesson
problem: Teachers share great lesson materials but earn nothing when others reuse them.
challenge: Counting a 'use' honestly without spying on classrooms.
direction: A paid API that licenses slide decks per lesson taught, paying the original teacher each time a deck is opened in class.
angles: What if adapted versions shared revenue with the original author?
Could schools in tight budgets be sponsored automatically?

title: Sponsor-funded homework helper
problem: Students without help at home fall behind on homework they could manage with small hints.
challenge: Letting sponsors fund help without them seeing who uses it.
direction: An Android app giving AI hints paid per question from a local sponsor pool, with no adverts and no tracking.
angles: What if the hint got smaller each time to encourage independence?
Could former students top up the pool?

title: Ask an alumnus, pay on answer
problem: Applicants have specific questions about courses that only recent graduates can really answer.
challenge: Holding the payment until a good answer arrives, and refunding if none does.
direction: A Next.js web app where applicants post a small held payment that releases only when an alumnus answers within two days.
angles: What if alumni could donate their earnings to bursaries?
Could the best answers become a free public FAQ?

title: Degree checks priced per lookup
problem: Employers wait weeks to confirm a candidate's qualifications with universities.
challenge: Charging per lookup while the graduate controls who may check.
direction: A paid API where employers pay per verification and graduates approve each request from a shareable link.
angles: What if graduates earned a share of each lookup?
Could a recruiter's agent check a whole shortlist in one go?

title: Bedtime story agent on pocket money
problem: Parents struggle to find stories pitched at exactly their child's reading level.
challenge: Buying stories chapter by chapter that stretch the child just enough.
direction: A Python agent that buys short levelled stories per chapter from independent authors, within a weekly budget a parent sets.
angles: What if the child chose how to spend the leftover budget?
Could authors write to order when the agent finds a gap?

title: Pay only when you learned it
problem: Learners pay for whole courses and abandon most of them halfway through.

angles: What if creators earned a bonus when learners passed weeks later?
Should the learner pay anything if the lesson was badly made?

title: Captions for village hall meetings
problem: Community meetings rarely offer live captions, so deaf residents miss local decisions.

angles: What if attendees could tip to upgrade to a human captioner?
Could the transcript become the meeting minutes?

title: Alt text per image, human on request
problem: Small websites publish hundreds of images with no descriptions for screen-reader users.
challenge: Knowing when AI alt text is good enough and when a person should write it.

angles: What if screen-reader users could flag poor descriptions for a refund?
Could the price depend on how complex the image is?

title: Easy-read version of any letter
problem: People with learning disabilities receive official letters they cannot understand alone.
challenge: Simplifying without dropping a single deadline or obligation.

angles: What if a support worker could approve the rewrite remotely?
Could the sender be billed instead of the reader?

problem: Charities know their websites fail accessibility checks but cannot afford a full audit.
challenge: Ranking fixes by real impact on users, not by how easy they are.

angles: How would you prove the money made the site better?
What if disabled testers were paid per issue confirmed?

title: Audio description on demand

angles: What if viewers could request description and the creator paid?
Could describers sell their voice style per clip?

title: Step-free route reports, paid per check
problem: Wheelchair users find out a route has a broken lift or high kerb only on arrival.
challenge: Keeping reports fresh when conditions change daily.

angles: What if local councils funded bounties for their own streets?
Could AI spot stale reports and raise the bounty?

title: Form-filling companion with a carer view

challenge: Turning a messy floor plan into something readable by touch.

angles: What if venues paid so every visitor could print one free?
Could the map update itself when a room moves?

title: Leaf photo diagnosis with a backstop
problem: Smallholders spot sick leaves but cannot reach an agronomist quickly.
challenge: Escalating to a paid human expert only when the AI is unsure.

angles: What if neighbouring farms shared one diagnosis for the same outbreak?
Could agronomists earn more for answering in the field season?

title: Satellite tiles bought field by field
problem: Farmers pay for whole-farm satellite subscriptions when only a few fields need watching.
challenge: Deciding which fields deserve a fresh image this week.
direction: A Python agent that buys single satellite tiles per field when crop signals look odd, staying inside a seasonal budget.
angles: What if a cloudy image was automatically refunded?
Could a cooperative's agents split the cost of shared tiles?

title: Soil report translator
problem: Soil test reports are full of numbers that growers find hard to act on.
challenge: Turning lab values into advice without overpromising yields.

angles: What if the lab paid so every report came explained?
Could allotment groups share one report across plots?

title: Farmer advice, tipped per useful answer
problem: Experienced farmers answer newcomers' questions in forums for nothing.
challenge: Rewarding answers that actually worked, not just the first reply.
direction: A Next.js web forum where askers tip answers and add a bonus later if the advice worked at harvest.
angles: What if an AI summarised the best tipped answers into a guide?
Could agricultural colleges sponsor tips for students' questions?

title: Herd sensor alerts sold per alert
problem: Livestock sensors produce floods of data that farmers and vets ignore.
challenge: Charging only for alerts that turn out to matter.

angles: What if consumers could scan for free and retailers paid?

challenge: Paying for counts without rewarding made-up numbers.

challenge: Streaming payment that matches energy delivered, not time plugged in.

title: Dishwasher agent that buys price forecasts

title: Energy bill decoder

angles: What if a debt-advice charity sponsored every explanation?

title: Office energy walkthrough agent

Could staff earn a share of the savings they spot?

problem: Festival-goers queue for phone charging and pay a flat fee even for a quick top-up.
challenge: Making per-minute charging simple for someone with a nearly dead phone.

angles: Should readings during a flood cost more or be free?
What if an agent bought readings only when rain was forecast?

challenge: Buying just enough supplier data to give an honest estimate.

What if suppliers earned something for each lookup of their data?

title: Sapling photos paid by sponsors

angles: What if rewards grew the longer a tree survived?

title: Repair-not-replace advisor

angles: What if companies could pay to have their own reports checked first?

When should it advise repairing rather than claiming?

title: Cashback that lands in seconds
problem: Loyalty schemes at independent shops are clunky cards that customers forget to bring.

angles: What if shops on the same street funded a joint reward?
Could the cashback grow on rainy days when footfall drops?

title: Prompts that earn per run

How would you stop someone reverse-engineering the prompt from outputs?

title: Agents hiring agents
problem: Specialist AI agents exist but cannot easily find or pay one another for sub-tasks.

Who decides a result failed when both sides are machines?

title: Lecture notes by the page

Could a lecturer endorse the best notes for a bonus?

title: Borrow a drill by the hour
problem: Neighbours buy tools they use once a year because lending feels awkward and risky.

Could lenders donate earnings to a street fund?

title: Voice lines on request
problem: Indie creators need a handful of human voice lines but hiring for a full session is overkill.

direction: A web marketplace where creators post individual lines and voice performers are paid per line accepted.
angles: What if a rejected take still earned a small fee?
Could listeners vote which take wins?

title: Hackathon credit shopper
problem: Hackathon teams waste the first hour comparing paid APIs and signing up for each one.

Should the agent favour cheap breadth or one deep tool?

title: Reverse auction for AI jobs
problem: Anyone with a batch AI job pays list price, even when spare capacity sits idle elsewhere.

angles: What if the job could be split across several winners?
How should the agent react when the cheapest bidder is unreliable?

title: Textbook price check

Could the price drop automatically as term approaches?

title: Parcel lockers rented by the hour
problem: Couriers waste trips when nobody is home, while shop back rooms sit half empty.

angles: What if the recipient paid extra for a closer locker?
Could slots be booked automatically by a courier’s route planner?

title: Proof-of-delivery photo checker
problem: Delivery photos are often blurry or show the wrong door, and disputes drag on.

angles: What if drivers got instant feedback before leaving the doorstep?
Could a good photo history lower a courier’s insurance?

title: Route agent that buys only doubt
problem: Small delivery firms cannot afford constant premium traffic data for every van.
challenge: Knowing when uncertainty is high enough to justify paying for an update.

angles: What if vans shared what they paid for with each other?
Should the agent spend more on deliveries with tight time slots?

title: Cold-chain alarm for food vans
problem: Small food traders lose whole loads when a fridge fails quietly on the road.

angles: What if the nearest cold store could bid to take the load?
Could the readings double as proof for a food inspector?

title: Customs forms with a refund promise
problem: Small exporters dread customs paperwork, and one wrong code can hold a shipment for days.

angles: What if experienced brokers reviewed tricky forms for a share of the fee?
Could the app learn from every rejection?

title: Empty space in the van
problem: Vans drive between towns half empty while people pay full price to move one sofa.

angles: What if the price dropped the closer the van got to leaving?
Could an AI estimate an item’s size from a photo?

title: Voice pick-list on a shift pass
problem: Temporary warehouse staff slow down while juggling paper pick-lists and scanners.
challenge: Charging for help only when it is actually being used.

angles: What if the app spoke the picker’s own language?
Could the warehouse pay only for minutes that sped picks up?

title: Late-parcel refund collector
problem: Online sellers are owed small refunds for late carrier deliveries but rarely claim them.

Should it ever decide a claim is not worth the cost?

title: Defect spotter per part
problem: Small workshops cannot afford inspection systems, so faulty parts slip out to customers.
challenge: Being reliable on parts the model has never seen before.

Could the price fall as the model learns a workshop’s parts?

title: Idle machines by the minute
problem: Makerspaces and workshops have laser cutters sitting idle while makers nearby have nowhere to cut.

angles: What if failed jobs were partly refunded automatically?
Could a student society book machines in bulk?

title: Maintenance agent with a diagnosis budget
problem: Small factories fix machines only after they break because expert diagnosis is costly.

angles: What if two factories with the same machine shared diagnoses?
How should it explain a spend that turned out unnecessary?

title: Spare parts licensed per print
problem: A broken plastic clip can write off an appliance because the part is no longer sold.

angles: What if repair cafés printed parts on behalf of visitors?
Could the original maker sponsor free prints of discontinued parts?

title: Safety briefings in every language
problem: On multilingual shop floors, safety briefings are understood by some workers and nodded through by others.
challenge: Translating technical safety language accurately enough to rely on.

Could the app flag phrases that translate badly?

title: Instant quotes from a drawing
problem: Engineers wait days for quotes on simple custom parts, and most requests never become orders.

angles: What if several workshops could beat the AI’s quote?
Should the fee rise for drawings that take longer to read?

title: Material certificate checker
problem: Goods-in staff accept metal deliveries on paper certificates that are rarely checked properly.

How should the app handle a certificate it cannot read?

title: Run the oven when power is cheap
problem: Small manufacturers pay peak electricity prices because rescheduling jobs by hand is too fiddly.

When is the forecast not worth buying at all?

title: Code review by the diff

Could the price drop for diffs that pass first time?

title: Flaky test detective
problem: Flaky tests waste hours because rerunning them enough times to be sure is expensive.

Should teams share findings for the same open-source library?

title: Docs free for humans, paid for bots

Could the earnings fund the docs writers directly?

title: Sponsor-funded API sandbox

Could unused calls be passed to another team?

title: Dependency thank-you jar
problem: Projects rely on dozens of free libraries whose maintainers see none of the value.

angles: What if the split favoured libraries with fewer funders?
Could a company match every student’s tip?

problem: On-call developers get alerts away from their desks and cannot dig into logs on a phone.

title: Free for people, metered for bots

angles: What if bot fees funded new datasets residents asked for?
Could a researcher apply for a sponsored allowance?

title: Quadratic funding for street projects
problem: Small neighbourhood projects lose out to whoever shouts loudest at the council.
challenge: Rewarding broad support over a few big donors while keeping it hard to game.

angles: What if backers could see their penny's matched value live?

title: Records request research agent
problem: Records requests return hundreds of scanned pages that nobody has time to read.

title: Street air quality, sold by the reading

title: Council notices in every community language
problem: Important notices about bins, roadworks and consultations reach many residents only in one language.

title: Thank-you tips for litter pickers
problem: Volunteer clean-up groups do visible good work but struggle to cover bags and gloves.

title: Fund one specific item
problem: Donors give to big general funds and never learn what their money actually bought.

problem: Developers want to give back, but one-off donations are easy to forget.

title: Surplus food matcher for food banks

challenge: Matching perishable food to collectors within hours, not days.

problem: Donors hesitate to give to small appeals that might never reach their target.

title: Easy-read versions of charity reports
problem: Charity reports are written for funders, not for the people the charity serves.

title: Bus fares back before you get home
problem: Volunteers on low incomes stop helping because expense claims take weeks to repay.
